title: “They pierced my hands and my feet” — the Hebrew prints the word the KJV renders “as a lion” at Isaiah 38:13
summary: The KJV of Psalm 22:16 has a verb: “they pierced my hands and my feet”. In the Leningrad Hebrew the word before “my hands” has no verb form; it is the word the KJV renders “as a lion” at Isaiah 38:13.
text: KJV Psalms 22:16: “For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.” Hebrew (WLC) 22:17: כָּ֝אֲרִ֗י יָדַ֥י וְרַגְלָֽי [as a lion / my hands and my feet]. For the same first word, KJV Isaiah 38:13: “as a lion, so will he break all my bones”. Hebrew (WLC) Isaiah 38:13: כָּֽאֲרִ֔י. Brenton’s Greek 21:17: ὤρυξαν χεῖράς μου, καὶ πόδας. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PSA021.htm) prints: “they pierced my hands and my feet”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/22/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/23/38/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA021.htm.
reasoning: The KJV clause has a verb of piercing with “my hands and my feet” as its object. The Hebrew edition prints, in that place, a single word before “my hands”, and the same letters are printed at Isaiah 38:13, where the KJV has “as a lion”. The Hebrew clause printed in Psalm 22 therefore has no verb of piercing between the previous clause and “my hands and my feet”. The Greek prints a verb and Brenton’s English renders it “pierced”, so the Greek and the KJV agree with each other and the difference is between the KJV and the Hebrew.
scope: T applies at Psalms 22:16 (Hebrew and Greek 22:17 and 21:17); the Hebrew edition quoted is the differing text. The Septuagint agrees with the KJV here and is not a differing witness. The record states what each text prints; it does not say which wording is original, does not say how the Hebrew clause is to be completed, and does not examine other Hebrew manuscripts. This compares the wording of the texts quoted. It does not show which wording is original. The passage is verse; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the speaker meant beyond the words quoted. The English quoted from Brenton’s own page is given only to show how that edition renders the Greek it prints; it is not a lexicon entry. The Hebrew and the Greek number this verse 17 because they count the psalm’s title as verse 1; Brenton’s Greek numbers this psalm 21 (KJV Psalm 22). title: “A little lower than the angels” — the Hebrew prints the noun the KJV renders “God” at Genesis 1:1

title: “The branch that thou madest strong for thyself” — the Hebrew and the Greek print “son”
summary: The KJV of Psalm 80:15 has “the branch” that God made strong. The Hebrew prints the noun the KJV renders “son” in “son of man” at 80:17, and Brenton’s Greek prints “son of man” at both places.
text: KJV Psalms 80:15: “And the vineyard which thy right hand hath planted, and the branch that thou madest strong for thyself.” KJV 80:17: “upon the son of man whom thou madest strong for thyself”. Hebrew (WLC) 80:16: וְעַל־בֵּ֝֗ן אִמַּ֥צְתָּה לָּֽךְ [and upon son / thou madest strong / for thyself]. Hebrew (WLC) 80:18: עַל־בֶּן־אָ֝דָ֗ם אִמַּ֥צְתָּ לָּֽךְ [upon son of man / thou madest strong / for thyself]. Brenton’s Greek 79:16: καὶ ἐπὶ υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου ὃν ἐκραταίωσας σεαυτῷ. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/PSA079.htm) prints: “and look on the son of man whom thou didst strengthen for thyself”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/80/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA079.htm.
reasoning: At 80:15 the KJV has “branch”. The Hebrew of the matching clause (80:16) prints the noun that the KJV renders “son” at 80:17, there followed by the word rendered “man”; at 80:16 it is not followed by a second noun. The Greek of 79:16 prints υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου, “son of man”, in the matching clause, which the Hebrew of 80:16 does not print as two words. So the English “branch” is a different word from the noun printed in both original-language texts.
scope: T applies at Psalms 80:15 (Hebrew 80:16, Greek 79:16). The Hebrew and the Greek both differ from the KJV’s “branch”; the Greek also prints “of man”, which the Hebrew of 80:16 does not print. title: “He will curse thee to thy face” — the Hebrew and the Greek print the verb of blessing
summary: The KJV of Job 1:11 and 2:5 has Satan say Job “will curse” God to his face. The Hebrew prints at both places a form of the verb whose passive form the KJV renders “blessed” at 1:21, and Brenton’s Greek prints the verb of blessing.
text: KJV Job 1:11: “and he will curse thee to thy face”. KJV Job 2:5: “and he will curse thee to thy face”. Hebrew (WLC) 1:11: אִם־לֹ֥א עַל־פָּנֶ֖יךָ יְבָרֲכֶֽךָּ [if not, to thy face he will bless thee]. Hebrew (WLC) 2:5: אִם־לֹ֥א אֶל־פָּנֶ֖יךָ יְבָרֲכֶֽךָּ. KJV Job 1:21: “blessed be the name of the Lord”. Hebrew (WLC) 1:21: יְהִ֛י שֵׁ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה מְבֹרָֽךְ [be the name of the Lord blessed]. Brenton’s Greek 1:11: ἦ μὴν εἰς πρόσωπόν σε εὐλογήσει. Brenton’s Greek 2:5: ἦ μὴν εἰς πρόσωπόν σε εὐλογήσει. Brenton’s Greek 1:21: εἴη τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου εὐλογημένον. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/JOB01.htm) prints at 1:11: “verily he will bless thee to thy face”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/1/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB01.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB02.htm.
reasoning: At 1:11 and 2:5 the KJV has the English verb “curse”. The Hebrew prints a form of the verb written with the letters of the word the KJV renders “blessed” at 1:21, and the Greek prints, at 1:11 and 2:5, a form of the verb it prints at 1:21 for blessing the name of the Lord. In the KJV the same Hebrew letters stand under “curse” at 1:11 and “blessed” at 1:21, which are English words of opposite direction.

title: “Ready to raise up their mourning” — the Hebrew prints the word the KJV renders “leviathan” at Job 41:1
summary: The KJV of Job 3:8 has those who curse the day “ready to raise up their mourning”. The Hebrew’s last word is the word the KJV prints “leviathan” at Job 41:1, and Brenton’s Greek prints “the great sea monster”.
